glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Because the Son is greater than the angels, His salvation must not be neglected; this Son shared our flesh and blood, tasted death for everyone, broke the devil’s power, and became a merciful and faithful High Priest who helps those who are tempted.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 2 completes the book’s first movement (1:1–2:18). Its opening “Therefore” draws the first warning straight out of chapter 1, and its closing verses introduce Jesus as High Priest, the theme Hebrews develops from 4:14 onward.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that He, by the grace of God, might taste death for everyone.” (Hebrews 2:9)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The chapter opens with a warning that grows out of everything chapter 1 said about the Son. “We must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away” (2:1). The danger Hebrews names is a slow drift through inattention. If the law spoken through angels carried real penalties, “how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation” (2:3)? The Lord Himself announced it, eyewitnesses confirmed it, and God bore witness with signs, wonders, miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Then Hebrews explains why the Son, who is above the angels, was made lower than them for a while. Psalm 8 speaks of humanity crowned with glory and set over God’s works, yet “now we do not yet see all things put under him” (2:8). What we do see is Jesus. He shared our lowliness, suffered death, and by the grace of God tasted death for everyone, and He is now crowned with glory and honor (2:9). Through suffering God made Him “perfect,” bringing Him to the goal of His calling as the captain who leads “many sons to glory” (2:10). He is not ashamed to call them brethren.

His death accomplished what no one else could. By sharing flesh and blood, He destroyed the devil’s power over death and set free “those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (2:15). Being made like His brethren in every way also made Him “a merciful and faithful High Priest,” who deals with sin before God and helps those who are tempted, because He Himself suffered when tempted (2:17–18).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 2:1–4 — Do Not Neglect So Great a Salvation

Because the Son is greater than the angels, believers must pay close attention to what they have heard, or they will drift away. If disobedience to the law brought a just penalty, there is no escape for those who neglect the salvation the Lord announced and God confirmed with signs and gifts of the Spirit.

Hebrews 2:5–9 — We See Jesus Crowned with Glory and Honor

Psalm 8 describes humanity’s calling to honor and rule over God’s works, a calling we do not yet see fulfilled. We do see Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels, who by God’s grace tasted death for everyone and is now crowned with glory and honor.

Hebrews 2:10–13 — The Captain of Salvation and His Brethren

God brought Jesus, the leader of our salvation, to the goal of His calling through suffering, as He brings many sons and daughters to glory. The One who makes people holy and those He makes holy belong to one family, and Jesus gladly calls them His brothers and sisters.

Hebrews 2:14–16 — Through Death He Destroys the Devil’s Power

Jesus took on flesh and blood so that through His death He could break the devil’s power and free those enslaved all their lives by the fear of death. His help is for the people of God’s promise to Abraham, not for angels.

Hebrews 2:17–18 — A Merciful and Faithful High Priest

Jesus was made like His brothers and sisters in every way so that He could be a merciful and faithful High Priest who makes atonement for their sins. Because He suffered when tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 2 shows that turning away from God’s salvation can begin quietly. People who have heard the gospel can slowly stop paying attention and drift (2:1). Hebrews warns that those who neglect “so great a salvation” will not escape (2:3). The greatness of the One who has spoken makes careful listening a matter of life and death.

The chapter also shows how close the exalted Son has come to His people. He did not save them from a distance. He took their flesh and blood, faced death, and suffered under temptation. Because of that, believers who fear death or struggle with temptation have a High Priest who understands and is able to help (2:14–18).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Do not drift. The greatness of the salvation spoken by the Lord demands careful attention (2:1–4).

Humanity’s calling fulfilled in Jesus. Psalm 8 finds its fulfillment in Jesus, crowned after tasting death for everyone (2:5–9).

The Son shares our humanity. Jesus took flesh and blood and calls His people brethren (2:11–14, 17).

Freedom from the fear of death. Jesus’ death broke the devil’s power and released captives (2:14–15).

A merciful and faithful High Priest. Jesus atones for sin and helps the tempted (2:17–18).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The word spoken through angels (2:2). The law given at Sinai, which Scripture associates with angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). Hebrews argues from the lesser to the greater: if that word carried real penalties, the salvation spoken by the Lord carries more.

Taste death (2:9). To experience death fully. Jesus truly died, and He did so on behalf of each person.

Captain of their salvation (2:10). The leader who goes ahead and brings His people to glory.

Perfect through sufferings (2:10). Jesus was always without sin (4:15). “Perfect” here means reaching the intended goal: through suffering He completed the path that made Him the Savior and High Priest of His people.

The seed of Abraham (2:16). The people of God’s promise to Abraham. Elsewhere Scripture shows that all who belong to Christ by faith share in that promise (Galatians 3:29).

Propitiation (2:17). Dealing with the people’s sins before God through an atoning sacrifice. Hebrews will show that Jesus made that sacrifice by offering Himself.

focus: Hebrews 2 turns the Son’s supremacy into a warning not to drift from so great a salvation, then explains why the Son was made a little lower than the angels. By sharing flesh and blood and tasting death for everyone, Jesus brings many sons to glory, breaks the devil’s power, and becomes a merciful and faithful High Priest who helps those who are tempted.

sections.title: Do Not Neglect So Great a Salvation
sections.summary: Because the Son is greater than the angels, “we must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away” (Hebrews 2:1). If the word spoken through angels brought a just reward for disobedience, there is no escape for those who neglect the salvation first spoken by the Lord, confirmed by those who heard Him, and attested by God with signs, wonders, miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

sections.title: We See Jesus Crowned with Glory and Honor
sections.summary: God has not subjected the world to come to angels, and Psalm 8 speaks of man made a little lower than the angels and crowned to rule over God’s works. We do not yet see all things put under him, but “we see Jesus” (Hebrews 2:9), crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone.

sections.title: The Captain of Salvation and His Brethren
sections.summary: In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God “to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” (Hebrews 2:10). He who sanctifies and those who are being sanctified are all of one family, and words from Psalm 22 and Isaiah 8 show that He is not ashamed to call them brethren.

sections.title: Through Death He Destroys the Devil’s Power
sections.summary: Since the children share flesh and blood, Jesus shared the same so that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death and release those held in bondage all their lives by fear of death. He gives aid not to angels but to “the seed of Abraham” (Hebrews 2:16).

sections.title: A Merciful and Faithful High Priest
sections.summary: Jesus had to be made like His brethren in all things so that He might be “a merciful and faithful High Priest” (Hebrews 2:17) and make propitiation for the sins of the people, dealing with their sins before God. Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to aid those who are tempted.

1.brief: Because the Son is so far above the angels, “we must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away.” The danger the writer names is not a sudden break but a slow drift that comes from failing to pay attention to God’s word in His Son.
1.explain: “give the more earnest heed” Therefore leads back to the Son’s superiority in chapter 1. The writer includes himself in the appeal to hold closely to the message the church has heard. A person can begin to drift by letting the truth slip out of attention and practice. The verse calls the whole congregation to take the Son’s word seriously now.

2.brief: The word spoken through angels, the law given at Sinai, proved steadfast, and every transgression and act of disobedience against it received a just penalty. Hebrews begins a lesser-to-greater argument: if that word carried such weight, the word spoken by the Son carries more.
2.explain: “the word spoken through angels proved steadfast” God’s law given at Sinai was binding, and Scripture associates angels with its delivery (Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19). Its penalties were just and showed that God held His people answerable for what He had spoken. That established accountability is the first half of the comparison.

3.brief: The writer asks, “how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation,” a salvation first spoken by the Lord Himself and confirmed to the writer and his hearers by those who heard Him. The question carries its own answer: since even the word spoken through angels brought a just penalty, as Hebrews 2:2 has said, those who neglect the salvation announced by the Lord will not escape God’s judgment.
3.explain: “how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation” If the word at Sinai carried consequences, those who neglect the greater salvation announced by the Lord will not escape God’s judgment. The Lord Himself first announced it, and firsthand hearers confirmed it to the writer and congregation. The greatness of the salvation and the authority of its Speaker give the warning its weight.

4.brief: God Himself bore witness to this message with signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His own will. The same God who spoke the word also confirmed it, which makes ignoring it all the more serious.
4.explain: “God also bearing witness” Alongside the human testimony stands God’s own confirmation. Signs pointed beyond themselves, wonders drew attention, and varied miracles and gifts showed the Spirit’s activity. God gave these demonstrations according to His will as witness to the message of salvation.

5.brief: God has not placed “the world to come, of which we speak” under the rule of angels. Hebrews turns from the warning back to its argument about the Son, preparing to show who will rule that coming world.
5.explain: “the world to come” God has not placed the coming world under angelic rule. This statement turns the argument from what angels helped deliver to who will exercise the rule God intends. Psalm 8 supplies the language for that next step.

6.brief: Hebrews quotes Psalm 8, where the psalmist asks, “What is man that You are mindful of him, Or the son of man that You take care of him?” The question marvels that the great Creator gives such attention and care to human beings.
6.explain: “What is man that You are mindful of him” Psalm 8 marvels that the Maker of the heavens pays attention to frail human beings. Its parallel question about the son of man deepens that wonder by speaking of God’s care. Hebrews begins with what the psalm says about humanity before turning to what it sees fulfilled in Jesus.

7.brief: The psalm continues that God made man a little lower than the angels, crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of His hands. Humanity was created for honor and for rule over God’s creation.
7.explain: “You have crowned him with glory and honor” Though placed below angels, humanity receives honor from God and a place of rule over what God made. The position is given to people by their Creator. Hebrews will show Jesus taking that human place and receiving its crown through suffering.

8.brief: God put all things in subjection under man’s feet and left nothing outside that rule, “But now we do not yet see all things put under him.” The writer admits the plain gap between humanity’s God-given calling and what we see in the world now.
8.explain: “He left nothing that is not put under him” The writer presses the public claim of the psalm: all things means all things. The authority God intended is greater than what we presently see human beings exercise. The words “not yet” leave the promise standing while preparing us to see where it is coming to fulfillment.

9.brief: What we do see is Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels and sharing our lowliness so that by the grace of God He might “taste death for everyone.” Because He suffered that death on behalf of each one, He is now crowned with glory and honor, and in Him humanity’s lost calling is being fulfilled.
9.explain: “But we see Jesus” Jesus entered our low position for a time. By God’s grace He truly tasted death for everyone, on behalf of each one. The Jesus who suffered that death is now crowned with glory and honor. He fulfills the human calling the psalm announces and opens the way for the many sons He brings to glory.
9.notes: The wording “a little lower” can convey a smaller degree of rank or a brief period of lowliness. Hebrews’ movement from suffering to crowning gives the time sense particular force as the words are applied to Jesus.

10.brief: In bringing many sons to glory, it was fitting for God, for whom and by whom all things exist, “to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.” Jesus’ suffering did not correct a flaw in Him but completed the path by which He became the leader who brings God’s people to glory.
10.explain:
“for whom are all things and by whom are all things” God is both the source and the goal of creation. The saving path He chose fits His purpose of bringing many sons to glory.

“perfect through sufferings” The captain is the leader who opens the way for those who follow. Jesus was already sinless. Through suffering He reached the intended end of the work God gave Him and became fully fitted to lead His people to glory as their Savior and High Priest.

11.brief: Jesus, the One who sanctifies, and those who are being sanctified “are all of one,” sharing one family and one Father, and so He is not ashamed to call them brethren. The holy Son gladly owns as His family the people He makes holy.
11.explain: “are all of one” The One who makes people holy and the people He makes holy belong to one family under one Father. The distinction between their roles remains. Jesus is the One who sanctifies, and His saving work gives Him reason to call them His own brothers and sisters openly.

12.brief: Hebrews places the words of Psalm 22 on Jesus’ lips: “I will declare Your name to My brethren; In the midst of the assembly I will sing praise to You.” The Son who suffered stands among His brothers and sisters to make God known and to praise Him with them.
12.explain: “In the midst of the assembly I will sing praise to You” In Psalm 22:22, the sufferer who has cried out to God now declares God’s name publicly among his brothers. Hebrews hears this as the voice of Jesus. The One who suffered stands with His family, makes God known to them, and joins them in praise.

13.brief: Jesus also speaks the words of Isaiah 8: “I will put My trust in Him,” and “Here am I and the children whom God has given Me.” He shares the trust in God that His people must live by, and He presents them as children God has given Him.
13.explain: “I will put My trust in Him” Hebrews presents Jesus as speaking the words of trust. In Isaiah 8:17–18 the prophet waits for the LORD and appears with the children God has given him. Hebrews applies that pattern to Jesus, who trusts God and stands with the children God has given Him. The two sayings make His solidarity with them concrete.

14.brief: Since the children share flesh and blood, Jesus Himself took on the same human nature so that through His own death He might destroy the devil, who had the power of death. By dying, Jesus broke the devil’s power over His people, the power that had held them captive through the fear of death.
14.explain: “He Himself likewise shared in the same” The children share flesh and blood, and the Son truly took on their mortal human condition. This enabled Him to die. Through His own death He broke the devil’s power over the people the devil had held through death and its fear.

15.brief: Through that death Jesus releases “those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.” The fear of death enslaves people throughout their lives, and Christ’s death sets them free from it.
15.explain: “all their lifetime subject to bondage” The fear of death can hold people captive throughout life. Christ’s death deals with the power that makes death a means of bondage, so His people can be released even while they still face physical death. The freedom follows from what their Savior has done on their behalf.

16.brief: Jesus does not give aid to angels, but He does give aid to “the seed of Abraham.” His help is for the people who belong to God’s promise to Abraham, which includes all who belong to Christ by faith.
16.explain: “the seed of Abraham” Jesus takes hold to help the people who have a share in God’s promise to Abraham. The contrast stays with the people He came to rescue rather than with angels. Galatians 3:26–29 explains how even Gentiles who belong to Christ by faith share in Abraham’s promised family.

17.brief: Therefore Jesus had to be made like His brethren in every way, so that He might be “a merciful and faithful High Priest” in matters relating to God and make propitiation for the sins of the people. Through His sacrifice He makes atonement for their sins, and this first use of the title High Priest in Hebrews joins His sharing of our humanity with that atoning work.
17.explain:
“in all things He had to be made like His brethren” Jesus shared the human condition of the people He represents. His mercy faces their need, and His faithfulness characterizes His service before God.

“to make propitiation for the sins of the people” He offers atonement that deals with their sins before God. This is the first explicit use of High Priest for Jesus in Hebrews, and it joins His true humanity to the saving work He performs for His people.

18.brief: Because Jesus Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted. His own experience of suffering under temptation makes His help real and timely for His people.
18.explain: “He Himself has suffered, being tempted” Jesus knows the pressure and suffering of temptation from experience. That gives substance to the help He can provide to people who are themselves under trial. Hebrews 4:15–16 keeps His sinlessness and His sympathy together, giving the tempted a reason to draw near for timely help.
